latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Loss of tolerance by B cells/plasma cells produces IgG, IgM, IgA, or mixed autoantibodies against red-cell surface antigens. This is the upstream driver across primary and secondary autoimmune hemolytic anemia; triggers modify probability and phenotype but are not part of the disease name.
IgG-coated red cells are cleared mainly by splenic macrophages, causing anemia, reticulocytosis, spherocytes, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, splenic enlargement, and low haptoglobin.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Complement fixation, C3 opsonization, and intravascular lysis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Antibody-triggered classical complement activation deposits C3d/C3b on red cells and can progress to intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, renal tubular injury, and more abrupt anemia.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Temperature-dependent red-cell agglutination and complement loading
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cold-reactive antibodies can agglutinate red cells in cooler peripheral circulation, promote complement deposition, and generate hemolysis that worsens with cold exposure and improves with warming.

Tissue hypoxia and erythropoietin drive reticulocytosis, macrocytosis, and polychromasia; inadequate compensation from marrow disease, infection, renal disease, folate deficiency, or antibodies to precursors makes anemia disproportionately severe.
Falling hemoglobin causes compensatory tachycardia, dyspnea, fatigue, syncope, myocardial demand ischemia, and organ hypoxia; baseline cardiopulmonary disease lowers the tolerance threshold.

Active hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, heme, microparticles, and inflammatory signals that increase venous and arterial thrombosis risk, especially during severe flares, hospitalization, splenectomy, malignancy, or steroid exposure.

Infections, systemic autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative or solid malignancy, transplantation, drugs, and immune checkpoint blockade can increase autoreactive B-cell activation or complement-fixing antibody production. This mechanism is modulated by context axes rather than being encoded in the disease name.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Secondary contexts increase the probability and persistence of pathogenic red-cell autoantibody production without changing the first-layer disease identity.
DAT detects immunoglobulin and/or complement coating patient red cells; it confirms mechanism but should not be required as presentation ranking evidence.
IgG red-cell coating is common in Fc-mediated extravascular hemolysis.
Complement-fixing antibodies deposit C3 fragments detectable by monospecific DAT.
IgG-coated erythrocytes bind macrophage Fc receptors and are cleared in spleen and liver.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: stronger when complement_mediated_hemolysis_context_probability or cold_reactivity_context_probability is high
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IgM and some IgG antibodies activate the classical complement pathway and load red cells with C3 fragments.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: active when cold_reactivity_context_probability and cold_exposure_trigger_context_activity are high
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Cold-reactive antibodies bind red cells at lower temperatures and promote agglutination and complement loading.
Red-cell destruction shortens RBC survival and lowers hemoglobin.
Loss of circulating red-cell mass lowers hematocrit in parallel with hemoglobin.
Accelerated red-cell clearance reduces measured RBC count.
Heme catabolism from extravascular hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin.
Total bilirubin rises as indirect bilirubin increases, sometimes with concurrent liver-trigger context.
LDH rises from red-cell destruction and tissue stress.
Haptoglobin is consumed binding free hemoglobin and is often very low in active hemolysis.
Partial phagocytosis of IgG-coated RBC membrane produces spherocytes.
Splenic macrophage activation and red-cell clearance may enlarge the spleen.
Terminal complement activity can lyse red cells intravascularly and release free hemoglobin.
Free hemoglobin filtered into urine produces dark urine or hemoglobinuria.
Hemoglobinuria and heme-mediated tubular toxicity can precipitate AKI during fulminant intravascular hemolysis.
Complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis consumes haptoglobin rapidly.
Intravascular lysis can produce abrupt LDH elevation.
Cold agglutinin titer tracks cold-reactive antibody burden, although thermal amplitude determines clinical activity.
Cold-reactive antibodies can cause visible red-cell agglutination in blood samples and smears.
Erythropoietin-driven marrow compensation releases reticulocytes.
Absolute reticulocyte count increases unless marrow reserve is impaired.
Corrected reticulocyte production index separates adequate compensation from reticulocytopenic severe AIHA.
Reticulocytosis commonly produces macrocytosis.
Polychromasia on smear reflects reticulocyte release.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: active when hemoglobin is substantially below patient-specific oxygen-delivery requirement
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Lower hemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery and activates physiologic compensation and organ stress.
Reduced oxygen delivery commonly presents as fatigue or malaise.
Anemia reduces oxygen carrying capacity and causes exertional dyspnea even without primary lung disease.
Tachycardia is a compensatory response to low oxygen content.
Profound anemia can trigger syncope, myocardial ischemia, shock physiology, or respiratory distress.
Active hemolysis, steroids, immobilization, malignancy, and splenectomy increase thrombotic risk.
Death in AIHA is often mediated by severe anemia with cardiopulmonary decompensation rather than by the diagnosis label itself.
AKI from hemoglobinuria worsens physiologic reserve and treatment complexity.
Pulmonary embolism, stroke, myocardial infarction, or splanchnic thrombosis are major causes of severe AIHA morbidity and mortality.
Complex crossmatch, alloantibodies, and emergency transfusion can add hemolytic or allergic transfusion risk, though lifesaving transfusion should not be withheld for severe symptomatic anemia.

Inflammatory/reactive thrombocytosis may accompany severe hemolysis or underlying inflammatory/malignant context; Evans syndrome can move in the opposite direction via separate context.
Reticulocytosis and mixed erythrocyte populations produce anisocytosis on smear.
Absolute reticulocyte count increases unless marrow reserve is impaired. Alternate reporting form represented separately from absolute/percent units.

axes.shape_free_text: Near-zero background; rises with hemoglobin collapse, cardiopulmonary decompensation, hemoglobinuria-AKI, thrombosis, transfusion complications, severe infection, or refractory secondary immune activation; falls when hemolysis is controlled and oxygen delivery restored.
Normal baseline; active AIHA ranges from mild anemia to life-threatening nadirs below 5 g/dL; recovery lags immune control and transfusion support.
Tracks red-cell mass; severe AIHA can produce hematocrit below 20%.
Falls with accelerated red-cell clearance; interpretation depends on transfusion and plasma volume.
Often normal to macrocytic because reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells; microcytosis suggests coexisting iron deficiency or thalassemia rather than AIHA itself.

Typically elevated after marrow compensation begins; may be inappropriately low in fulminant early disease, marrow failure, renal insufficiency, infection, folate deficiency, or precursor-directed autoimmunity.
Absolute reticulocytosis can exceed several hundred x10^9/L in brisk compensation.
Corrected marrow response; values above 2 indicate compensation, while low values in severe anemia indicate inadequate production.
Usually elevated in hemolysis; very high values suggest abrupt intravascular hemolysis or additional tissue injury.
Low or undetectable in active hemolysis; may be falsely normal or high with inflammation because haptoglobin is an acute phase reactant.
Rises with indirect bilirubin; can be amplified by hepatic injury or cholestasis context.
Preferentially elevated in hemolysis; disproportionate direct bilirubin suggests concurrent hepatic or biliary disease.
Usually less elevated than indirect bilirubin in isolated AIHA; increases when viral hepatitis, cholestasis, sepsis, or liver disease is present.
Normally very low; rises with intravascular hemolysis and complement terminal pathway activity.
DAT/Coombs positivity reflects red-cell coating by Ig and/or complement; confirmatory and subtype-context information, not presentation-only ranking evidence.
Monospecific DAT IgG result; confirms antibody pattern and treatment context.
Monospecific DAT C3d result; identifies complement-loaded red cells and helps modulate complement-directed strategies.
Usually absent/low; clinically relevant cold-reactive disease has elevated titer and broad thermal amplitude, but titer alone is not severity.
Spherocytes support Fc-mediated extravascular hemolysis; not specific because hereditary spherocytosis can mimic it.
Agglutinated red cells on smear or analyzer flags support cold-reactive antibody effect.
Polychromasia reflects reticulocytosis from marrow compensation.
Scleral icterus or jaundice from bilirubin rise; severity depends on hemolysis and liver context.
Clinical pallor tracks anemia severity but has exam variability.
Dark urine may reflect hemoglobinuria or high urobilinogen; strongest for intravascular/complement hemolysis.
Common anemia symptom; nonspecific and best interpreted with hemolysis labs.
Exertional dyspnea or respiratory distress from anemia; amplified by lung or heart disease.
May rise with severe anemia, fever, infection trigger, or cardiopulmonary stress.
Usually normal in isolated anemia despite low oxygen content; low values indicate respiratory/cardiac comorbidity or critical illness.
Normal in primary flares; fever suggests infection, systemic autoimmune activity, malignancy, transfusion reaction, or inflammatory context.
May be present with extravascular hemolysis or underlying lymphoproliferative/infectious context; absence does not exclude AIHA.
Can reflect reticuloendothelial clearance, infection, malignancy, or liver disease context.
Risk of syncope, myocardial ischemia, heart failure, shock physiology, or critical hypoxia from severe anemia.
Risk of AKI from intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, dehydration, shock, or nephrotoxic context.
Risk of venous or arterial thrombosis during active hemolysis, hospitalization, malignancy, steroid exposure, and especially peri/post-splenectomy.
Risk added by complex serology, alloantibodies, emergency incompatible transfusion, and high transfusion burden; lifesaving transfusion may still lower net mortality through hemoglobin rescue.
Context axis indicating IgG/Fc-dominant hemolysis; derived from serology, thermal amplitude, smear, and clinical course, not from disease name.
Context axis for complement-dominant hemolysis, DAT C3d positivity, cold-reactive hemolysis, or intravascular features; modulates warming and complement inhibition.
Context axis for cold-reactive antibody behavior; modulates steroids, warming, complement inhibition, and sample handling.
Current environmental or procedural cold exposure risk; not a disease subtype.
Context axis for drug-associated immune hemolysis; used to strengthen withdrawal strategy and avoid re-exposure.
Context axis for immune-checkpoint inhibitor exposure temporally compatible with AIHA; supports discontinuation/immune-toxicity management.
Context axis for malignancy-associated immune activation; informs need for malignancy-directed therapy in addition to hemolysis control.
Context axis for SLE and other systemic autoimmune disease activity; modulates recurrence risk and steroid-sparing strategy.
Context axis for acute or chronic infection temporally associated with AIHA; not ranking evidence for AIHA unless independently observed.
Context axis for Evans-like concurrent immune thrombocytopenia or neutropenia; changes bleeding, infection, and immunosuppression tradeoffs without redefining AIHA.
Probability that compatible or least-incompatible RBC transfusion can be delivered promptly with adequate blood bank support.
Composite risk from uncontrolled infection, diabetes, delirium, severe psychiatric disease, osteoporosis, or frailty; modifies steroid harm but not disease identity.
Composite risk from HBV core antibody, chronic viral infection, severe hypogammaglobulinemia, active infection, or profound immunosuppression.
Composite operative and long-term infection/thrombosis risk; modified by age, cardiopulmonary reserve, thrombosis history, vaccination feasibility, and active hemolysis.
Host reserve axis: coronary disease, heart failure, severe lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, or advanced frailty lowers tolerance to anemia.
WBC is often normal in isolated AIHA but may rise with infection trigger, immune checkpoint toxicity, inflammation, steroid exposure, or underlying malignancy.
Neutrophil count is context dependent; neutrophilia can accompany inflammatory/drug-triggered AIHA while neutropenia suggests Evans/marrow overlap.
Platelets are often preserved in isolated AIHA but may be low with Evans syndrome or high with inflammation, malignancy, or steroid response.
Lymphocyte count varies with EBV/CMV trigger, lymphoproliferative context, immune activation, or treatment context rather than being primary hemolysis.
AST may rise mildly to moderately from hemolysis, hepatic stress, infection trigger, or transfusion/ischemic context.
ALT may rise when AIHA is triggered by viral/drug/systemic inflammatory contexts or accompanied by hepatic stress.
Peripheral smear anisocytosis reflects mixed red-cell populations, reticulocytosis, transfusion, and active hemolysis context.
Reticulocyte percentage; separate from absolute reticulocyte count because percent and 10^9/L are not interchangeable without RBC count.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The immediate danger of AIHA is often mediated by low oxygen-carrying capacity rather than hemolysis markers alone.
Anemia-related syncope, myocardial ischemia, shock physiology, and respiratory distress raise death hazard.
Both reflect hemolysis intensity after common mechanism edges are accounted for.
Hemolysis can rise quickly, while marrow compensation and reticulocytosis lag by days.
Hemoglobinuria is the clinical sign that free hemoglobin is reaching renal tubules.
AKI increases critical illness risk and constrains transfusion/immunosuppression management.
Thromboembolism is a major preventable severe outcome in active hemolysis and after splenectomy.
Transfusion complexity adds risk, but this must be balanced against immediate hemoglobin rescue by forward simulation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fc-mediated extravascular hemolysis commonly improves with glucocorticoid suppression of macrophage clearance and autoantibody production.
Cold/complement-dominant hemolysis is less steroid-responsive than IgG/Fc-dominant disease.
Uncontrolled infection, severe diabetes, delirium, and frailty increase steroid harm.

side_effects.interpretation: Dose- and duration-dependent bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infection risk.
Steroid hyperglycemia; magnitude depends on diabetes risk.
Steroids can add thrombosis risk during active hemolysis and hospitalization.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid immune suppression for active hemolysis, especially Fc-mediated presentations.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Complex autoantibody or alloantibody workup can delay compatible or least-incompatible RBC delivery.
Symptomatic hypoxic anemia gains immediate survival benefit from oxygen-carrying capacity restoration.

side_effects.interpretation: Alloantibody, autoantibody masking, or emergency least-incompatible transfusion adds reaction risk.
Risk rises in elderly patients, heart failure, renal impairment, and rapid multi-unit transfusion.

treatments.context_specific_role: Immediate oxygen-delivery support for symptomatic or profound anemia while immune-directed therapy takes effect.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit is strong when pathogenic B-cell clones are CD20-sensitive but incomplete when a non-B-cell tumor or plasma-cell driver dominates.
HBV reactivation, hypogammaglobulinemia, or active infection can dominate harm unless mitigated.

side_effects.interpretation: B-cell depletion can cause late neutropenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and bacterial/viral infection.
Requires HBV screening and prophylaxis when relevant.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing or relapse-preventing B-cell suppression; too slow to replace immediate transfusion or acute rescue in critical anemia.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IVIG can transiently saturate Fc-mediated clearance in selected severe cases.
High-dose IVIG can increase thrombosis and viscosity risk.

side_effects.interpretation: High-dose IVIG can increase thrombotic risk, especially in active hemolysis or vascular disease.
Osmotic nephrosis and renal stress risk depend on product and host kidney reserve.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporary bridge in severe immune hemolysis while slower therapies start working.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Complement inhibitors directly target complement-dominant hemolysis and add little when Fc-only hemolysis dominates.
Complement blockade increases susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria; vaccination and prophylaxis may be needed.

side_effects.interpretation: Highest concern for meningococcal and other encapsulated infections depending on complement target.

treatments.context_specific_role: For complement-dominant hemolysis context when hemolysis is clinically significant or refractory to non-complement measures.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Avoiding cold exposure reduces peripheral agglutination and complement fixation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Non-pharmacologic trigger control and safe transfusion handling in cold-reactive context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Plasma exchange can transiently reduce circulating antibody and complement mediators in fulminant intravascular hemolysis.

side_effects.interpretation: Citrate anticoagulation can cause symptomatic hypocalcemia.
Central venous access and anticoagulation add procedural bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporary bridge for fulminant intravascular/complement hemolysis or life-threatening refractory anemia while definitive immune control is arranged.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Splenectomy targets splenic Fc-mediated red-cell clearance.
Complement/liver-mediated clearance is less spleen-dependent.
Operative, infectious, and thrombotic risk may outweigh durable benefit.

side_effects.interpretation: Lifelong encapsulated bacterial infection risk after splenectomy.
Perioperative and long-term thrombosis risk rises after splenectomy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Durable reduction of spleen-mediated red-cell destruction when medical control is inadequate and surgical risk is acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: When AIHA tracks systemic autoimmune activity, disease-modifying immunosuppression can reduce recurrence.
Broad immunosuppression can worsen active infection-trigger contexts.

side_effects.interpretation: Myelosuppression depends on agent, dose, TPMT/NUDT15 status, and renal function.
Broad immunosuppression raises bacterial, viral, and opportunistic infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Slower maintenance or refractory control when steroid dependence or systemic autoimmune context requires durable immune modulation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stopping the causal medication can remove the immune trigger.
Treating the infection or allowing viral trigger resolution can reduce immune drive.
Tumor-directed therapy may remove a paraneoplastic or clonal B-cell driver.

side_effects.interpretation: Toxicity depends on the underlying context therapy, such as antimicrobial, chemotherapy, surgery, or immune-related adverse event management.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduce a removable upstream trigger while AIHA-specific rescue stabilizes hemolysis and oxygen delivery.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active hemolysis and hospitalization increase thrombosis risk; prophylaxis lowers event hazard when bleeding risk is acceptable.
Severe immune thrombocytopenia or active bleeding can make pharmacologic prophylaxis unsafe.

side_effects.interpretation: Bleeding risk depends on platelet count, renal function, active bleeding, and procedure needs.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduce hemolysis-associated thrombotic events when platelet count and bleeding context permit.

female.trajectory_modulation: Autoimmune disease background modestly enriches AIHA probability.

risk_factors.factor: Older age or limited cardiopulmonary reserve

elderly_or_low_reserve.clinical_rationale: The same hemoglobin nadir is less tolerated with coronary disease, heart failure, lung disease, or frailty.

risk_factors.factor: Drug or immune checkpoint inhibitor exposure

present.clinical_rationale: Absent compensation during active hemolysis produces faster oxygen-delivery failure and may indicate marrow disease, infection, renal EPO deficiency, or precursor-directed autoimmunity.

risk_factors.factor: Prior transfusion or pregnancy alloimmunization context

present.clinical_rationale: Alloantibodies do not cause AIHA but complicate blood bank support and can mimic or coexist with autoimmune hemolysis.

risk_factors.factor: Renal impairment or dehydration during intravascular hemolysis

supportive_care: Coordinate early with transfusion medicine; rule out alloantibodies, phenotype/genotype when possible, and provide antigen-matched or least-incompatible RBCs when anemia is life-threatening.
Do not let complex crossmatch delay emergency oxygen-delivery rescue when severe symptomatic anemia is driving hypoxia hazard.
Give folate supplementation during sustained hemolysis and monitor for folate deficiency during reticulocytosis.
Trend CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, LDH, indirect/total bilirubin, haptoglobin, creatinine, urinalysis for hemoglobinuria, and DAT pattern when clinically needed.
Assess cardiopulmonary reserve, symptoms, ECG, troponin, and volume status in profound anemia, especially elderly or coronary disease patients.
Use warmed samples, warmed blood products, and cold avoidance precautions when cold-reactive context is suspected or confirmed.
Hydration and renal monitoring during intravascular hemolysis; avoid nephrotoxins and adjust IVIG or anticoagulation strategy for kidney function.
Evaluate thrombosis risk during active hemolysis and hospitalization; use mechanical or pharmacologic prophylaxis when bleeding and platelet context allow.
Screen for and treat removable triggers such as drugs, infections, systemic autoimmune activity, lymphoproliferative disease, solid tumor, or immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity.
Before rituximab or prolonged high-dose steroids, screen HBV, HCV, HIV, TB risk, immunoglobulin level when appropriate, and provide antimicrobial prophylaxis or vaccination according to risk.
Before splenectomy, vaccinate for pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b when feasible; plan lifelong fever/sepsis education and prophylaxis strategy.
Monitor steroid toxicity: glucose, delirium, psychiatric symptoms, blood pressure, infection, GI bleeding risk, bone protection, and myopathy.
Avoid unnecessary platelet transfusion or anticoagulation changes unless concurrent immune cytopenia, active bleeding, or thrombosis context makes them clinically necessary.

Document DAT/Coombs pattern, cold agglutinin titer/thermal amplitude, drug exposure, transfusion history, and underlying context as confirmatory or treatment modifier information, not as direct presentation ranking evidence.
